# Shiny apps for open-ended exploration {#sec-shiny}

The apps in the earlier chapters run in your browser. This chapter has two
**Shiny** apps that run on your own computer, using the real R packages
(`survival`, `ggsurvfit`, `MatchIt`, `cobalt`). They are for free
exploration after the guided chapters.

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## In this chapter
**By the end of this chapter you will be able to:**

- download and run the two Shiny apps on your own computer;
- use real datasets to practise KM curves, log-rank tests, Cox models and
  proportional hazards checks;
- compare matching, weighting and covariate adjustment on simulated data,
  and see when each one struggles.
:::

## Running the apps

1. Download the apps into your project folder (see @sec-setup):
   - [survival-explorer.R](apps/survival-explorer/app.R){download="survival-explorer.R"}
   - [psm-explorer.R](apps/psm-explorer/app.R){download="psm-explorer.R"}
2. Make sure the packages are installed (see @sec-setup), including
   `shiny`.
3. Run an app from the RStudio console. It opens in a new window:

```r
shiny::runApp("survival-explorer.R")
shiny::runApp("psm-explorer.R")
```

To stop an app, close its window and press **Esc** in the console (or click
the red stop sign).

## App 1: survival explorer

[Download survival-explorer.R](apps/survival-explorer/app.R){download="survival-explorer.R"}

Three real datasets from the `survival` package: `lung`, `veteran` (a
randomised lung cancer trial) and `colon` (an adjuvant chemotherapy trial).

- **Kaplan–Meier tab.** Choose a grouping variable. Toggle confidence
  intervals, risk tables and the median. Shows the log-rank test.
- **Cox model tab.** Choose any set of covariates. Shows a table of HRs and
  a forest plot.
- **PH check tab.** `cox.zph()` tests and Schoenfeld residual plots.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Suggested activities
1. In `veteran`, compare the *treatment* groups by KM. Then fit a Cox model
   with `treatment`, `celltype` and `karno`. Check PH. `karno` clearly
   violates it. What would you do? (Hint: @sec-nonph-example.)
2. In `colon`, compare `rx` arms. Is the Lev+5FU effect still there after
   adjusting for `nodes` and `differ`? (It's a randomised trial, so it
   should be.)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answers
1. **veteran.** The KM curves for the two treatments cross and the log-rank
   test is far from significant ($\chi^2 = 0.008$). In the Cox model, the
   Test treatment HR is about 1.30, not significant. `cox.zph()` flags
   **`karno`** (p < 0.001) and **`celltype`** (p ≈ 0.002). The effect of
   performance status is strong early on and fades over time. Options are
   `strata(celltype)` and a time-varying effect for `karno`, e.g. split
   follow-up with `survSplit()` or use `tt(karno)`.
2. **colon.** Without adjustment, Lev+5FU vs observation has HR ≈ 0.69
   (95% CI 0.55–0.87), and levamisole alone has HR ≈ 0.97. Adjusting for
   `nodes` and `differ` barely changes this (HR ≈ 0.67), as you'd expect in
   a randomised trial. Adjustment can improve precision, but it shouldn't
   move the estimate much. (`differ` shows some evidence of non-PH. Worth a
   look in the PH tab.)
:::

## App 2: propensity score explorer

[Download psm-explorer.R](apps/psm-explorer/app.R){download="psm-explorer.R"}

Simulates the observational cohort from Chapters 5–7, with adjustable
sample size, true HR and **strength of confounding**. You can then:

- choose which confounders go into the PS model (leave one out to create an
  *unmeasured confounder*);
- choose **1:k nearest-neighbour matching** (ratio, replacement, caliper)
  or **inverse probability weighting**;
- see balance (Love plot and PS distributions) for *all* true confounders,
  matched or weighted KM curves, and a comparison of HRs from the naive
  analysis, full covariate adjustment and the PS method, against the truth.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Suggested activities
1. Set confounding to 3. Compare 1:1 matching with no caliper, 1:1 with a
   0.2 caliper, and IPTW. Look at balance, sample size (or effective sample
   size) and the HR.
2. Untick `age`. Age is the strongest confounder, so balance on age
   collapses and every PS estimate is biased.
3. Set the true HR to 1 and confounding to 2. How wrong is the naive
   analysis?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answers
With the default seed (2026), true HR 0.7:

1. **Confounding = 3.** The naive HR is about 1.75. With 1:1 matching and
   no caliper, every treated patient is matched, but the |SMD| for age is
   still about 1.0. The matched HR is about 1.65, barely better than the
   naive one. With the 0.2 caliper, only 468 of 972 treated patients are
   kept. Balance is much better, though age is still just over the
   threshold (SMD ≈ 0.11). The HR is about 0.83, still a bit biased. IPTW
   also gives about 0.83, but the largest weight
   is about 60 and the effective sample size falls to roughly a third.
   **When the groups barely overlap, every method struggles.** Full
   covariate adjustment (0.74) does best here because the outcome model is
   correctly specified, which you can never guarantee in real data.
2. **Untick `age`** (confounding = 1). Age is no longer balanced, and the
   matched HR jumps to about 0.98, so the benefit disappears completely.
3. **True HR = 1, confounding = 2.** The naive HR is about 2.0, which looks
   like a doubling of risk from a treatment that does nothing. The matched
   estimate is about 1.02, close to the truth.
:::

## Going further (optional, for instructors): running a Shiny app in the browser
Shiny apps can also run with no R installed, using
[shinylive](https://posit-dev.github.io/r-shinylive/) and webR. Put the
downloaded file in its own folder, renamed to `app.R`. Then run:

```r
# install.packages("shinylive")
shinylive::export("survival-explorer", "site/survival-explorer")
httpuv::runStaticServer("site/survival-explorer")
```

Not every CRAN package is available in webR, so test the app before you rely
on it.
:::
::::
